California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted more than 900,000 signatures and qualified with over 600,000 valid signatures, above the 546,651 required for an initiated statute. It qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. The Legislative Analyst lists exactly this—whether the program increases construction and homebuying—as an open question. That uncertainty is the heart of the trade-off.
Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].
The assistance is tied to newly built homes and paired with a builder option, so the design at least aims at expanding supply rather than only subsidizing demand [1, Sec. 51515.02].
The program lowers the down-payment barrier, the largest single obstacle for many first-time buyers, by covering up to 17 percent of the price [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)].
It carries real consumer protections. The loans must be fixed-rate, origination fees are capped, prepayment penalties are barred, and lenders face agency-set consumer rules [1, Sec. 51515.04].
The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?
If the loan pool underperforms, who actually bears the loss, and could the state face pressure to step in despite the no-liability language?
Does a ceiling of 200 percent of the area median income target the households with the greatest need or does it spread the subsidy to higher earners in costly counties?
How much of the subsidy reaches buyers as lower costs, and how much is captured by builders and sellers through higher new-home prices?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
This measure promises help for middle-class buyers at no cost to taxpayers. That is true only if borrowers repay $25 billion in bonds in full. Ask who is left holding the loss if they do not and whether a state agency running a program this large could really stand aside.
A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a new home only improves affordability if it also gets more homes built. Ask whether this measure will add enough new supply to keep from simply bidding up the price of the homes it covers.

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted more than 900,000 signatures and qualified with over 600,000 valid signatures, above the 546,651 required for an initiated statute. It qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. The Legislative Analyst lists exactly this—whether the program increases construction and homebuying—as an open question. That uncertainty is the heart of the trade-off.
Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].
The assistance is tied to newly built homes and paired with a builder option, so the design at least aims at expanding supply rather than only subsidizing demand [1, Sec. 51515.02].
The program lowers the down-payment barrier, the largest single obstacle for many first-time buyers, by covering up to 17 percent of the price [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)].
It carries real consumer protections. The loans must be fixed-rate, origination fees are capped, prepayment penalties are barred, and lenders face agency-set consumer rules [1, Sec. 51515.04].
The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?
If the loan pool underperforms, who actually bears the loss, and could the state face pressure to step in despite the no-liability language?
Does a ceiling of 200 percent of the area median income target the households with the greatest need or does it spread the subsidy to higher earners in costly counties?
How much of the subsidy reaches buyers as lower costs, and how much is captured by builders and sellers through higher new-home prices?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
This measure promises help for middle-class buyers at no cost to taxpayers. That is true only if borrowers repay $25 billion in bonds in full. Ask who is left holding the loss if they do not and whether a state agency running a program this large could really stand aside.
A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a new home only improves affordability if it also gets more homes built. Ask whether this measure will add enough new supply to keep from simply bidding up the price of the homes it covers.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.

Updated

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.

Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.

Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.

About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.

Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.

While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.

About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.

Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.

Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide.
