When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

I've got enough evidence now, and it points toward Yes winning Prop 37. The latest polls have it ahead, and there's no organized opposition or spending against it.

I'm weighing the risks for a "No" outcome: the ballot is crowded with 14 props, and unfamiliar voters often default to No. Even so, with 65% backing Yes in polling and only 32% No, undecided voters would have to break heavily against it to flip the result. I'm also checking how past propositions that polled similarly ended up, and the outcomes landed close to their poll numbers.

Still weighing a late check: whether any group ran a last-minute campaign against Prop 37, which seems unlikely. I'm also considering whether post-election results are indexed by searching for the governor's race outcome.

37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026
Republish

In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.

If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/)
Get ready for California’s midterm election. This voter guide has everything you need to know
Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique (https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/determining-the-price-impact-of-harris-down-payment-assistance-proposal/) of down payment assistance programs.
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf) commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026) highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure.
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans.
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7% (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/business/interest-rates-economy-markets-inflation-mortgages.html). Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber).
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.
But Hertzberg said he has a plan.
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards (https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/cra_about.htm).
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion (https://players.brightcove.net/876630612001/2eCBwdutJ_default/index.html?videoId=6406972609112), Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited.
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.
For the record: This story was corrected to note that Prop. 37 loans could be used to purchase any home sold under the policy’s specified price cap, even if the builder is not part of the “qualified builder” program.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Voters will decide on proposals to tax billionaires, extend taxes on high earners, fund biomedical research and more on the November general election ballot (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide). Here’s everything you need to know about all the California propositions:
Proposition 1
The basics
Proposition 1 asks voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion through the sale of bonds to build and maintain housing that low- and middle-income residents can afford. It’s called the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 1: Borrowing money for low-income and veteran housing (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-1-affordable-housing-voter-guide)
Prop 1 guide: Lawmakers are asking voters to let the state borrow $11.25 billion to build and maintain housing low- and middle-income residents can afford.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The largest chunk of this money — $7.2 billion — would be doled out as loans to builders who agree to rent some of the homes to low-income families; in Los Angeles County, a family of four earning about $133,000 a year qualifies as low-income. Researchers recently found (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf) that the construction of nearly 40,000 low-income homes was in limbo because of a lack of funding.
Advertisement
The second-largest portion of these funds — $1.25 billion — would be set aside for housing for veterans, in the form of homeownership loans. Voters last approved this type of statewide bond for veteran home loans in 2018.
Dig deeper
Proposition 1 is supported by Democrats and organizations that provide low-income housing, plus various municipal governments. They say it is key to helping more Californians achieve homeownership. Republicans oppose it, saying the state should curtail building regulations to bring down the cost of housing without burdening taxpayers.
Proposition 2
The basics
Proposition 2 would give government the ability to put more money into savings and create another option for leaders to avoid triggering taxpayer rebates during future budget surpluses.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 2: Lets leaders fatten ‘rainy day’ fund, reduces likelihood of taxpayer rebates (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-2-rainy-day-fund-voter-guide)
Prop 2 guide: California Democrats want to change the state constitution to allow them to deposit more money into budget reserves, creating another option to avoid giving excess revenue back to taxpayers.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
The measure exempts deposits into state savings accounts from a spending limit that voters previously adopted through a series of ballot measures dating to the late 1970s, and increases the share of general fund tax revenue that can be put aside in reserves.
Dig deeper
Democrats say the changes will allow the state to save more when the economy is growing and use the funds to lessen cuts to vital programs during bad times. Republicans say it will allow the state to spend more money that otherwise would go back to taxpayers.
Proposition 3
The basics
There has been much debate about efforts in California to tax the rich. But almost all of it centers around Proposition 40, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) the heavily contested billionaire tax, and two countermeasures, Propositions 41 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide) and 42. (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
But Proposition 3 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) — getting far less attention — also would tax California’s wealthiest citizens and has even garnered support from some billionaires who oppose Proposition 40. The proposition would make permanent an expiring state income tax on high earners.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 3: Making a high-income tax extension permanent (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 3 would make permanent an expiring income tax on the top 2% of California taxpayers that provides money for education, healthcare and other services.
Oct. 1, 2026
The impact
Tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers. Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Dig deeper
In 2012, California voters approved a temporary increase in the income tax rate for the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030. Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
Advertisement
Backers say the measure is crucial to maintain education funding levels and predict there would be grave problems if the measure is not approved.
The state could expect to lose from $5 billion to $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Opponents say taxes are already too high and the state should focus on cutting waste.

## Proposition 37: A $25 billion state loan program for middle-income homebuyers

# Proposition 37 would set aside $25 billion to help Californians buy new homes
California’s November ballot includes Proposition 37, proposing a down payment assistance program to help low- to middle-income Californians purchase newly constructed homes.
Proposition 37 would allow California’s Housing Finance Agency to borrow upwards of $25 billion to provide low-interest loans at 17% of a home’s value to potential homebuyers.
By covering a majority of the down payment, the loan leaves buyers paying only 3% of a downpayment upfront.
The home must be newly built, and eligible buyers can earn a maximum of twice their area’s median income.
For example, in the city of San Luis Obispo, buyers could not earn more than $147,000 annually to remain eligible, according to the Census Data.
The proposition would not increase taxes for Californians and funding would come from selling state revenue bonds to private investors, according to the voter guide.
State revenue bonds are used to finance state projects by asking investors to purchase a bond, according to the California State Treasure’s Office.
For Proposition 37, these bonds would be paid back by the assisted homebuyers paying off their down payment loan.
Supporters, including the California Democratic Party and the California Association of Realtors, believe this proposition will open the door to homebuyers who would otherwise be unable to afford a down payment.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . California’s Prop.

Learn how the middle-class housing measure works and its key caveats.
Oct. 24, 2026
**The impact**
The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down-payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages.
Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building.
The proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure was approved.

Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
Supporters say restricting the program to new homes could spur construction.
But critics warn down-payment debt could burden buyers and that Proposition 37 does little to address a bigger issue: the cost of building.

## Proposition 37: Creates a loan program for middle-income homebuyers
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a state homebuying assistance program for eligible middle-income Californians purchasing newly built homes.
The program would provide fixed-rate loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying home's purchase price.
Eligible buyers would have to meet income requirements, occupy the home as their residence and make a down payment of at least 3%.
A yes vote would establish the program and authorize the bonds.
A no vote would prevent the state from being required to create it.
The measure's proponents say it would make homeownership more accessible without directly relying on taxpayer-funded bond repayments.
The bonds would be repaid through borrowers' mortgage payments.
No formal opposition argument was submitted against the measure, though at least one critic, the League of Women Voters, has said Proposition 37 would fail to confront racial barriers to wealth-building and lower overall costs for families.

# Proposition 37: Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
## What does California Proposition 37 do?
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos.
These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home.
Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders.
Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible.
Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default.

Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2037.pdf)

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute” (as prepared by the attorney general). The attorney general’s summary reads that it “authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a ‘qualified new home.’”
Measure’s own name: California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0013A1)
Type: Initiated state statute. It adds a new chapter to the Health and Safety Code. It is not a constitutional amendment [1, SEC. 2].
A vote YES means: The California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) could issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund below-market second mortgages that cover up to 17 percent of the price of a newly built home for moderate-income buyers, repaid out of those buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
A vote NO means: No such program is created. CalHFA continues its existing, smaller homebuyer and down-payment programs, and no new $25 billion bond authority is granted.
Sponsor/proponent: Robert M. (Bob) Hertzberg, former State Senate majority leader and former Assembly Speaker, through the California Homes Coalition. The California Association of Realtors supports the measure.
On the ballot because: Proponents submitted more than 900,000 signatures and qualified with over 600,000 valid signatures, above the 546,651 required for an initiated statute. It qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office, Proposition 37 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 37 would create a state-run second-mortgage program for moderate-income Californians buying newly built homes. It directs the California Housing Finance Agency to establish the Middle-Class Homeownership Loan Program and authorizes the agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund it [1, Sec. 51515, 51515.06].
The core mechanic is a second, or “secondary,” mortgage. A qualifying buyer would still take out a normal primary mortgage from a private lender. On top of that, the state program would provide a fixed-rate second loan covering up to 17 percent of the purchase price, the share ordinarily covered by a down payment. The buyer must still put in at least 3 percent of their own money [1, Sec. 51515.05(b), 51515.01(a)(1)(D)]. The second mortgage is a loan, not a grant. The buyer repays it, and those repayments are what pay back the bond investors over time.
To qualify, a buyer must have lived in California for at least one year, must occupy the home as a primary residence within sixty days of closing, and must have family income no higher than 200 percent of the area median income for their county [1, Sec. 51515.01(a)(1)]. The home must be a “qualified new home,” meaning newly constructed housing where the buyer is the first purchaser, or a formerly nonresidential building converted to housing. Its price cannot exceed 125 percent of the federal conforming loan limit for the county, which works out to roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on location, adjusted annually [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
The measure also tries to pull new supply into the market. It creates a voluntary “qualified builder option” with labor and enforcement conditions attached, and it states as a purpose the expansion of single-family home construction to address California’s housing shortage [1, Sec. 51515(a), 51515.02]. The Legislative Analyst estimates the program could support construction in the range of tens of thousands of homes, though the actual number is uncertain.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0013A1, “California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) (amended version submitted September 22, 2025)
Key language:
“Each middle-class homeownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage and shall … finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent.” [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)]
“This bond shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California, other than the agency, but shall be payable solely from the funds provided therefor.” [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]
What it amends: It adds Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 51515) to Part 3 of Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, the division that governs CalHFA [1, Sec. 2]. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature may amend it without a return to the voters, but only by a vote of more than 60 percent of each house and only in ways consistent with the measure’s purposes [1, Sec. 3].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by former State Senate majority leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg through the California Homes Coalition, with support from the California Association of Realtors. The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency. The beneficiaries would be moderate-income buyers of newly built homes, private lenders who originate the loans, and homebuilders who opt into the builder program.
What? Up to $25 billion in CalHFA revenue bonds funding fixed-rate second mortgages of up to 17 percent of a new home’s price, repaid from buyers’ loan payments rather than from taxes.
Where? Statewide, administered by CalHFA, with per-county price caps tied to the federal conforming loan limit [1, Sec. 51515.01(b)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the agency must stand up the program within one year of the effective date [1, Sec. 51515.05(a)].
Why? The stated goals are to make home financing more affordable for middle-class buyers, expand single-family home construction, and do so “with no cost to taxpayers” by repaying the bonds through homeowner loan payments [1, Sec. 51515(a)(1)-(2)].
4. Trade-offs
Most California bond measures authorize general obligation bonds, which the state repays out of the general fund, so every dollar borrowed carries decades of taxpayer-funded interest. Proposition 37 authorizes revenue bonds instead. The bonds are payable solely from the homebuyers’ loan repayments and carry an explicit statement that they are not a debt or a pledge of the state’s faith and credit [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)]. On that basis the Legislative Analyst concludes there would be “no direct state or local costs.” That claim is accurate as far as it goes. The interest on up to $25 billion of borrowing is still real, but it is designed to be carried by the borrowers who benefit, not by the general taxpayer.
The big question is what “no cost to taxpayers” hides. The promise holds only if the loan pool performs. If defaults and losses run beyond the program’s reserves, the legal text puts that loss on bondholders, not the general fund. But a $25 billion program that carries the state’s name and is run by a state agency could generate strong political pressure for a rescue if it faltered, whatever the fine print says. Analysts call this a moral-obligation or contingent risk. It is not a certainty, and the measure is drafted to avoid it, but it is the reason “no cost to taxpayers” deserves an asterisk rather than a period.
The deeper economic question is whether the program raises affordability or raises prices. A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a home increases demand. If the supply of homes does not increase, that added demand tends to be capitalized into higher prices, so part of the subsidy ends up in the pockets of sellers and builders rather than buyers. This is the standard critique of down-payment assistance, and it is why the measure’s design matters. Proposition 37 does not subsidize any home. It subsidizes newly built homes and adds a builder option meant to pull new construction into the market [1, Sec. 51515.02]. If that supply response is large, the price-inflation worry shrinks. If builders do not respond and the subsidy simply chases a capped pool of new homes, the measure could bid up the price of the very homes it targets. The Legislative Analyst lists exactly this—whether the program increases construction and homebuying—as an open question. That uncertainty is the heart of the trade-off.
Two more points should be considered. First, the below-market promise depends on investor appetite. To sell $25 billion in bonds while keeping homebuyer interest rates low, the spread has to come from somewhere, and the Legislative Analyst flags investor demand as an unknown. Second, the income ceiling is generous; 200 percent of area median income in an expensive county can exceed a quarter-million dollars for a family, so a “middle-class” subsidy would reach some relatively high earners.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
The bonds are revenue bonds repaid from homeowner loan payments, not general obligation bonds. Unlike a typical bond measure, this creates no scheduled general fund debt service [1, Sec. 51515.06].
The assistance is tied to newly built homes and paired with a builder option, so the design at least aims at expanding supply rather than only subsidizing demand [1, Sec. 51515.02].
The program lowers the down-payment barrier, the largest single obstacle for many first-time buyers, by covering up to 17 percent of the price [1, Sec. 51515.05(b)].
It carries real consumer protections. The loans must be fixed-rate, origination fees are capped, prepayment penalties are barred, and lenders face agency-set consumer rules [1, Sec. 51515.04].
The program is designed to qualify for federal Community Reinvestment Act credit, which could draw private lending into underserved communities [1, Sec. 51515(a)(4), 51515.03(b)].
Potential risks
The “no cost to taxpayers” claim holds only if borrowers repay in full. Large losses fall on bondholders under the text, but a failing $25 billion state-branded program could invite pressure for a state backstop [1, Sec. 51515.06(b)].
If new construction does not actually expand, subsidizing demand for a capped set of new homes could raise their prices, capturing part of the benefit for sellers and builders.
Delivering below-market mortgages while paying competitive bond yields depends on investor demand that the Legislative Analyst treats as uncertain.
The 200 percent of area median income ceiling directs a large subsidy toward relatively high earners in expensive counties, which weakens the “middle-class” targeting.
The agency’s program rules are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act, and the legislature can amend the measure by a 60 percent vote, so the usual public rule making and voter-approval checks are reduced [1, Sec. 51515.05(a), Sec. 3].
6. Open questions
Will the qualified-builder option meaningfully expand new-home supply, or will it mostly subsidize buyers of homes that would have been built anyway?
Can CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds at rates low enough to deliver below-market mortgages without drawing down its reserves?
If the loan pool underperforms, who actually bears the loss, and could the state face pressure to step in despite the no-liability language?
Does a ceiling of 200 percent of the area median income target the households with the greatest need or does it spread the subsidy to higher earners in costly counties?
How much of the subsidy reaches buyers as lower costs, and how much is captured by builders and sellers through higher new-home prices?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
This measure promises help for middle-class buyers at no cost to taxpayers. That is true only if borrowers repay $25 billion in bonds in full. Ask who is left holding the loss if they do not and whether a state agency running a program this large could really stand aside.
A subsidy that lowers the cost of buying a new home only improves affordability if it also gets more homes built. Ask whether this measure will add enough new supply to keep from simply bidding up the price of the homes it covers.

California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17%
Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026

California's Proposition 37 is asking voters to let the state lend new-home buyers up to 17% of the purchase price
Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency borrow up to $25 billion from investors and lend it to buyers of newly built homes as a second mortgage covering up to 17% of the price. The buyer puts in at least 3%, a conventional first mortgage covers the rest, and the state loan is repaid monthly at a fixed rate that the agency sets high enough to pay the bondholders back. Anyone who has lived in California for a year and earns no more than twice the area median income can apply, with no first-time-buyer requirement. The home must be new, the buyer must be its first owner, and its price cannot exceed 125% of the county's conforming loan limit, which works out to about $1.04 million in 41 counties and about $1.56 million in the ten most expensive ones in 2026. The Legislative Analyst's Office finds "no direct state or local costs," because borrowers' payments, not the General Fund, repay the bonds.
The Middle-Class Homeownership Loan under Proposition 37 is covering 17% of an $800,000 home so the buyer's own cash drops from $160,000 to $24,000. Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the best-polling of them: 61% yes to 35% no in PPIC's September survey. No argument against it was filed, no opposition committee exists, and its Yes side reports $30.9 million from top donors, led by the state's Realtors, the carpenters' unions and the Brin-and-Doerr-funded Building a Better California. Governor Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and the California Democratic Party support it, the California Republican Party is neutral, and the editorial boards split two to two. This explainer covers what the text does, who qualifies and at what price, how the loan compares with the help CalHFA already offers, the builder option, the consumer rules, the cost, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers up to 17% of a new home's price:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a chapter to the Health and Safety Code directing CalHFA to run a "Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program" and authorizing it to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, the kind repaid by the program's own income rather than by the state. Each loan "shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price" and must be secured by a second mortgage behind the buyer's primary loan. The agency has to launch the program within one year of the measure taking effect, and it decides how many bonds to sell and when, "in a manner that minimizes interest costs and encourages broad investor participation."
The repayment design is in section 51515.05. CalHFA sets the interest rates, amortization schedules and payment terms "on terms the agency determines practical and favorable to applicants and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds," plus "all costs of administration." The loans must be fixed-rate, the agency may let a borrower use the loan for closing costs if that "balances the interests of borrowers and bond investors," and every bond must state on its face that it "shall not be deemed to constitute a debt or liability or a pledge of the faith and credit of the State of California." The Legislative Analyst's Office (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/analysis.htm) notes that CalHFA "also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible," and that the measure leaves the rate itself to the agency.
The program is restricted to new homes. A "qualified new home" is a newly built house, townhome, row house, condominium or manufactured home, or a unit in a former nonresidential building converted to housing, in either case "where the borrower is the first purchaser." Builders may sell qualified homes to anyone; only buyers using the loan must meet the program's rules. The measure also says these homes are not "public works," so prevailing-wage law does not attach to them by default, and it lets CalHFA write its program rules without going through the Administrative Procedure Act, subject to its own board.
